We also describe supporting infrastructure for dataset validation, curation, standardized event annotation, and scalable cohort-level analysis. Finally, we provide practical recommendations emphasizing standardized data organization, complete reporting of analysis parameters and software environments, code sharing, preregistration, automated quality control, and robustness analyses across plausible pipelines. Together, these practices provide a foundation for EEG findings that are more transparent, reproducible, and generalizable across datasets, laboratories, and analytical tools.
authors: Takfarinas Medani; Raymundo Cassani

title: Designing sustainability under Earth-system rate constraints
summary: Sustainability debates are monopolized by quantities: total energy use, material stocks, or recycling volumes. These metrics are informative, but they obscure a more fundamental constraint. On a materially closed but energetically open Earth, long-term viability is governed by rates: power density, areal power density, and the rate at which dispersed materials can be repurified under dif- fuse solar fluxes. We develop a physical framework that links technological metabolism, material dilution, and recycling limits through these rate con- straints. This perspective clarifies why many contemporary technologies remain viable only through stock drawdown and high-power buffering, and why green growth strategies often shift rather than resolve the underlying mismatch between industrial activity and Earth-system dynamics. We argue that long-term sustain- ability requires both quantitative reduction in aggregate industrial throughput toward rate-bounded regimes and the development of technologies qualitatively compatible with biospheric operating conditions.
authors: José Halloy; Petros Chatzimpiros; François Graner; Thomas Gregor

title: Two-dimensional framework for modeling load transfer in nanocomposites with thin, stiff, and prestressed reinforcements
summary: This paper presents a novel framework for simulating load-transfer mechanisms in nanocomposites reinforced by thin, stiff, and prestressed reinforcements, such as, e.g., nanosheets or nanoplatelets. The reinforcements are modeled as open material surfaces treated as membranes endowed with their own elastic properties and residual surface tension; the matrix is assumed to be isotropic elastic. In the two-dimensional plane-strain setting considered here, each material surface is represented by a sufficiently smooth curve of otherwise arbitrary shape. The theoretical part of the framework is based on the Gurtin--Murdoch theory in which the surfaces are represented by traction jumps across them. The elastic fields in the matrix are exactly expressed by the integral representations written in terms of the unknown traction jumps that are functions of the second-order derivatives of the displacements. The computational part is based on the isogeometric boundary element method (IGABEM) that utilizes non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS). The unknown traction jumps are found from the numerical solutions of the coupled system of singular boundary integral equations, after which the elastic fields in the matrix are evaluated. The procedure of extracting the values of the stress intensity factors (SIFs) at the tips of the surfaces is described. The proposed algorithm is validated against available benchmark solutions for multiple surfaces located along either straight segments or circular arcs. Selected parametric studies are performed to examine the influence of surface curvatures, relative spacing, orientation, and interactions. An example involving a graphene nanoplatelet-reinforced epoxy is presented.
authors: Rohit Satish Patil; Zhilin Han; Sofia G. Mogilevskaya

title: Scalar-Longitudinal Modes of Extended Electrodynamics in Perfectly Conducting Cavities and Trapped Modes of Divergence Cleaning
summary: In extended electrodynamics, the Lorenz condition is not imposed and $C=\nabla\cdot\mathbf{A}+μ_0\varepsilon_0\partialΦ/\partial t$ is a dynamical field, which adds a scalar-longitudinal (SL) family to the TE, TM and TEM modes of a cavity. With $C=0$ on the wall of a closed perfectly conducting cavity, the classical resonances remain unchanged, while the SL modes are the Dirichlet eigenmodes of the volume, with $\mathbf{B}=0$ and an electric field along $\nabla C$. In uniform cavities they share the frequencies of the TM modes that vary along the axis, and for a connected wall the fundamental remains classical. Matching at a conductor described by its constitutive laws gives $\partial C/\partial n=0$ instead and couples the scalar-bearing modes to the Maxwell field. The results belong to the $C=0$ problem, the condition that separates the sectors and the one divergence cleaning imposes. The rectangular, circular cylinder and coaxial cavities provide benchmarks, together with the damping time that gives the slowest scalar mode its fastest decay.
authors: Natan Rentzber; Jacob Howard; Fernando Minotti; Anatoliy Pinchuk; Giovanni Modanese

title: Nonreciprocal magneto-optic beam steering of thermal emission
summary: Conventional thermal emitters obey Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation, which ties absorptivity to emissivity and places a fundamental limit on a range of radiative energy technologies and sensing systems. This constraint can be overcome using magneto-optic materials, which exhibit nonreciprocal thermal emission under an applied magnetic field. While the spectral nonreciprocity of magneto-optic devices has been explored theoretically and experimentally, nonreciprocal control over the direction of thermal emission has received far less attention. Here, we propose and numerically demonstrate nonreciprocal beam steering of thermal emission, wherein an applied magnetic field lifts the degeneracy between guided modes at +/- kx, enabling asymmetric and tunable directional thermal emission. We highlight a III-V semiconductor photonic structure operating at 24.5 um, a wavelength with few laser sources. This structure exhibits a nonreciprocity greater than 0.5 between +/- 75 degrees at 50 mT, a peak emissivity asymmetry over 0.6 at 150 mT, and 22 degrees of beam steering between 0 and 1 T. Our approach provides a solid-state means of steering a thermal beam, offering a potential route to magnetically controlled beam scanning of incandescent sources.
authors: Mason Christiansen; Daniel Cui; Aaswath P. Raman

title: Compressive microendoscopy in the presence of noise and misalignment: the translational correlation advantage of graded-index fibers
summary: Multimode fibers (MMFs) offer a minimally invasive platform for deep-tissue and multisite in vivo optical sensing. Computational microendoscopy methods extend them into the high-resolution imaging domain, but are quite sensitive to experimental errors. This study investigates the robustness of microendoscopy based on compressive sensing (CS) by comparing step-index (SI) MMFs with graded-index (GRIN) fibers. Mode-expansion-based simulations are used to assess the accuracy of image reconstruction in the presence of fundamental photon noise and lateral fiber shifts. We show that both fiber types exhibit comparable noise sensitivity, but GRIN fibers are significantly more robust to lateral misalignment errors. These results establish GRIN MMFs as an alignment-tolerant platform for robust computational microendoscopy.
authors: M. S. Pochechuev; T. I. Rajib; A. Dharmasiri; A. M. Zheltikov

title: Interplay Between Network Heterogeneity and Activation Thresholds in Global Cascades
summary: The onset of global cascades in complex networks depends on both the distribution of activation thresholds and the underlying network topology. Here we investigate how these two sources of heterogeneity interact within the Watts threshold model, using beta-distributed activation thresholds and beta-binomial degree distributions to systematically vary their respective properties. Analyzing the onset of cascades from infinitesimal seeds, we identify two distinct boundaries governing the large-connectivity behavior of vulnerable branching. The first separates regimes in which increasing connectivity enhances or suppresses propagation, depending on the abundance of individuals with low activation thresholds. The second distinguishes two mechanisms of suppression: one controlled by the scarcity of low-threshold individuals and the other by the diminishing abundance of low-degree nodes as connectivity increases. At the boundary between these mechanisms, their competing contributions produce a logarithmic correction to the asymptotic scaling. Our results demonstrate how the interplay between network structure and individual activation thresholds determines the conditions for extensive propagation.
authors: Aidan Meador-Woodruff; Gourab Ghoshal

title: Neural Eigenfluid Bases: Spectral Objectives, Gauge, and Topology
summary: Reduced-order models simplify fluid simulation by representing complex flows with a small number of spatial modes. Building on Laplacian Eigenfluids, we introduce Neural Eigenfluid Bases (NEB), a neural representation whose basis functions can be evaluated anywhere in space. We enforce incompressibility and impermeable boundaries directly through differential lifts and potential boundary conditions. Geometry-local orthogonalization and Rayleigh minimization then learn an ordered basis. We connect learning in potential and velocity spaces, and derive a spectral-variance relation explaining why these objectives weight approximate modes differently, even though their exact positive spectra agree. Gauge fixing reduces the number of spatial derivatives needed for potential learning, while a Dirichlet energy loss learns independent circulation fields around obstacles. With 1024 modes, both objectives keep velocity errors below 1% in periodic vortex merger. For random flows around obstacles, potential-based learning captures more initial energy and gives lower final errors than numerical Laplacian bases of the same size. The reduced state is about a thousand times smaller than the full reference model. Three-dimensional tests separate spatial reconstruction errors from errors in coefficient evolution. Precomputed Galerkin operators allow millisecond-scale updates when the same basis is reused across simulations. This provides a physically constrained basis for continuous flow reconstruction and efficient reduced-order simulation.
authors: Baiming Zhang; Shiying Xiong; Zhecheng Wang

title: Generalization of the Rosenbluth-Putvinski avalanche growth rate to the drift kinetic regime
summary: A new collisionless detrapping mechanism is shown to modify the rate of runaway electron (RE) generation by as much as a factor of two for strong inductive electric fields. This detrapping mechanism results from the magnetic well inherent to tokamak geometry being tilted by the strong inductive electric fields present during tokamak disruptions. The impact of this collisionless detrapping mechanism is found to be described by a single dimensionless parameter, whose identification enables the transition between distinct regimes of RE generation to be characterized. Using this composite parameter, it is shown that modifications to the avalanche growth rate by tokamak geometry across a broad range of plasma parameters collapse onto a one-dimensional curve that can be accurately fit with a two parameter function. The resulting analytical formula extends the classic Rosenbluth-Putvinski avalanche growth rate expression beyond the bounce-averaged limit into RE regimes where collisionless detrapping strongly modifies RE generation rates.
authors: Christopher J. McDevitt; Jonathan S. Arnaud

title: Surface Functionalization with Lasers: from Nanostructures to Applications
summary: Pulsed laser sources stand out as remarkable and versatile tools in the growing interdisciplinary field of materials science, offering capabilities for tailoring and customizing materials to meet specific requirements. Their ability to induce different controlled material alterations allows enhancing material properties that might otherwise remain elusive. In essence, laser-induced material modifications encompass a spectrum of transformative processes, ranging from subtle topographical changes in the nano- and microscale, to intricate chemical modifications. Among the challenges to overcome are the creation of approaches that allow tuning the properties of light to optimize interactions on various types of solids, including metals, semiconductors, and dielectrics. Understanding these interactions is paramount towards efficiency increase of the processing techniques. This chapter embarks on a comprehensive exploration of the intricate dance between pulsed laser beams and their interaction with matter at the surface. The applications of laser-induced surface modifications are far-reaching and extend into widespread industrial fields. Examples of these include tribology, where the study of friction, wear, and lubrication is paramount. Besides that, the modified surfaces find applications in wetting phenomena, changing surface energy and contact angle control, enhanced welding processes, and optimizing molecular adhesion for stronger and durable interfaces. The ability to precisely engineer material surface properties through laser processing opens new frontiers in materials and surface sciences, offering innovative solutions and pushing the boundaries of what can be achieved in various industrial and technological domains.
authors: Bastian Zielinski; Martin Kahlmeyer; Stefan Böhm; Jörn Bonse; Camilo Florian

title: Non-Hermitian Topology of a Subwavelength Resonator in Synthetic Space
summary: Non-Hermitian singularities and the nontrivial topology of energy bands have been extensively explored in extended periodic systems, where phenomena such as exceptional points and bulk Fermi arcs are naturally associated with periodicity and momentum space. Here, we show that this non-Hermitian topology can be extended to the domain of subwavelength resonators using a synthetic space. By reconstructing the complex energy bands of a subwavelength ring resonator in the synthetic space of geometrical parameters, we experimentally observe a spectral triplet formed by two exceptional points (EPs) connected by a bulk Fermi arc and a topologically robust quasi-bound state in the continuum (q-BIC). This Fermi-arc q-BIC emerges exactly at the intersection of the bulk Fermi arc and the q-BIC line in synthetic space, establishing a direct topological link between two spectral singularities. Encircling the EPs in synthetic space visualizes the nontrivial topology of the complex energy-band structure and reveals the opposite half-integer topological charges of the EPs connected by the bulk Fermi arc. These results extend non-Hermitian topology to subwavelength structures and establish compact resonators as a versatile platform for applications in photonics, microwave physics, and acoustics.
authors: N. Solodovchenko; F. Zhang; M. Bochkarev; K. Samusev; M. Song; M. Limonov; A. Bogdanov

title: Accurate measurement of Lithium Tantalate birefringence in whispering gallery resonators
summary: Lithium Tantalate (LTA) is an important ferroelectric crystal widely used in piezoelectric, electro-optic, and nonlinear optical devices. Although this crystal is very common, there is an ongoing debate regarding its birefringence magnitude, and even its sign. While some sources claim it to be negative, others maintain that it is positive. The issue is further complicated by the sample-to-sample variation in the crystal composition, ranging from congruent to stoichiometric. Here we report the experimental exploration of this question based on high-resolution spectroscopy of optical whispering gallery resonators fabricated from this crystal. These sensitive measurements unambiguously indicate that in the near-infrared range at room temperature the stoichiometric LTA is negative, while the congruent LTA is positive.
authors: Linjie Shao; Andrey B. Matsko; Anatoliy A. Savchenkov; Harald G. L. Schwefel; Nicholas J. Lambert; Florian Sedlmeir; Dmitry V. Strekalov

title: Energy cascades in atmospheric moist convection
summary: We analyze scale-by-scale budgets of velocity and buoyancy second-order structure functions using Large Eddy Simulation of the BOMEX trade-wind cumulus layer. The simulation utilizes a $10\,\mathrm{m}$ grid resolution under the anelastic approximation, incorporating moist thermodynamics to capture phase changes. The analysis of derived turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) and turbulence potential energy (TPE) budgets reveals four regions of distinct turbulence dynamics. For three of these regions, approximate balances holding over wide range of length scales are identified, highlighting the importance of interspace and pressure transport. Above the lifting condensation level ($\approx 800\,\mathrm{m}$), phase changes introduce forcing across all resolved scales, leading to an inverse TPE cascade spanning all scales. The TKE, inter-scale transfer is inverse above the vertical velocity integral length scale but below the horizontal velocity scale. In the upper cloud layer ($>1400\,\mathrm{m}$), forward inter-scale transfers are recovered despite ongoing phase changes. A phenomenological interpretation of these features, referring to the different formation stages of convective updrafts, is also proposed. Finally, 1D horizontal subsamples from the simulation show good agreement with recent airborne measurements, validating the numerical framework and confirming the departure of moist convective turbulence from standard energy cascade models.
authors: Paweł Jędrejko; Marta Wacławczyk; Benjamin Luce; Szymon P. Malinowski; Jakub Nowak; J. Christos Vassilicos

title: Dynamical systems analysis of Bianchi type-IX cosmology with a scalar field mediated dark sector interaction
summary: The recent DESI DR2 results preference for a time-varying dark-energy equation of state, together with the long-standing difficulty of explaining why an initially anisotropic universe should evolve toward isotropy, motivates the study of interacting dark-sector models in anisotropic backgrounds. We investigate the dynamics of Bianchi type-IX cosmologies containing pressureless dark matter coupled to dark energy in the form of a quintessence scalar field $φ$ with exponential potential $V(φ)=V_0\,e^{-λφ}$. Energy exchange between the two dark components is mediated by the scalar field through the interaction term $Q=κβ\dotφ\,ρ_{\rm DM}$, where $κ^2=8πG$ and $β$ is a dimensionless coupling. Because Bianchi~IX models generically recollapse, the Hubble scalar $H$ vanishes at the moment of maximum expansion, where the expansion-normalized variables of the standard Wainwright--Ellis formalism diverge. We therefore adopt the $D$-normalized phase-space formalism of Hewitt, Uggla, and Wainwright, which compactifies the state space and remains regular through the recollapse, including the moment of maximum expansion at which $H = 0$. Together with the modified conservation equations for the two dark components, the Einstein equation reduces to a closed autonomous polynomial dynamical system, whose fixed points we classify by linear stability analysis, supplemented by center-manifold theory for the non-hyperbolic points. The fixed points shows the kinetic-dominated, coupling modified matter dominated, curvature scalar, scalar field dominated and coupled scaling families; the last is the anisotropic analogue of the Amendola scaling attractor. Restricting to the initially expanding, isotropizing trajectories, we map the region of the $(λ,β)$ plane in which anisotropic Bianchi~IX models approach an accelerating Friedmann--Robertson--Walker state.
authors: Ashmita; Jaturaporn Watanakampolkij; Daris Samart

title: Cutting Corners or Saving Lives? The Evolutionary Stability of Ethics in Pharma Medicine
summary: The pharmaceutical industry operates at the intersection of financial incentives, state oversight, and public scrutiny. We model corporate compliance with a three-population replicator system of ethical firms, active regulators, and active public scrutiny, whose payoffs are motivated by a prisoner's dilemma of first-mover advantage, an inspection game between firms and the FDA, and a volunteer's dilemma in early-stage research. The eight payoff constants are fitted by bounded L-BFGS-B optimization to composite indices for 2010--2024, and a fully sourced dataset of fifteen heavily penalized firms links the model's strategy types to R&D intensity and penalties. The calibrated system has no interior fixed point: an exact identity shows that public scrutiny decays at a rate set by the difference between the regulators' and the public's cost-to-benefit ratios. Without public scrutiny the firm--regulator dynamics are conformally Hamiltonian, so the two populations cycle neutrally around a center, and Lyapunov exponents give no evidence of chaos. Bureaucratic friction $k$, which enters compliance costs as $k^3$, organizes two thresholds: above $k^*\approx0.75$ regulators saturate and compliance rests on public scrutiny, and above $k^{**}\approx0.81$ compliance collapses. The empirical friction index crosses both between 2016 and 2020, as the compliance index falls from $0.85$ to $0.60$. Relative to revenue, penalties are highest for the firms with the lowest R&D intensity. Ethical compliance is therefore an oscillating rather than a permanent state, persisting only while friction stays below the combined incentive of subsidies, fines, and public penalties.
authors: Alanna Polyak; Thomas Zdyrski

title: Non-Ideal Relativistic Plasma Mirrors
summary: Relativistic plasma mirrors formed in the wake of intense laser pulses propagating in underdense plasmas can provide an efficient mechanism for generating attosecond pulses, and for enhanced focusing towards ultra-high intensity fields. We derive the reflection coefficient of a laser pulse interacting with relativistic mirrors, assuming different density profiles for the mirror. Analytical expressions are obtained for flat-top and parabolic density mirrors, and in the Dirac-delta limit, demonstrating the strong dependence of the reflectivity on the plasma mirror density profile. Fully kinetic multi-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations and our analytical model confirm that the density spike at the rear of the plasma bubble exhibits an approximately parabolic profile. Our results show that a laser wakefield setup can be optimized to maximize the reflection coefficient under specific laser driver conditions, determined by the balance between the moving plasma mirror proper density, thickness, and relativistic momentum carried by the mirror.
authors: Zahra M. Chamazkoti; Luís O. Silva

title: Wave-branch classification of ideal MHD discontinuities in Q-variables
summary: The $Q$-variable formalism combines velocity and magnetic field into branches aligned with a selected MHD wave. For homogeneous ideal MHD, appropriate choices of the branch parameter $α$ correspond to the fast, Alfvén, and slow characteristic families, with the background variables $\boldsymbol{Q}_0^{\pm}$ representing the propagation direction and speed of the corresponding characteristics. In structured plasmas, $α$ may instead be selected from the dispersion relation of a global mode such as a kink wave. Recent work reformulated the ideal-MHD Rankine-Hugoniot conditions in $Q$-variables and established their exact equivalence with the classical conservative jump conditions. Here, we apply this formulation to the standard ideal-MHD discontinuity catalogue. We determine how the two discontinuity-frame branches $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\prime+}$ and $\boldsymbol{Q}^{\prime-}$, their sums, and their $α$-normalised differences are constrained across contact, tangential, and rotational discontinuities and across the principal shock families. Material interfaces are distinguished by their normal branch content, rotational discontinuities by an Alfvénic tangential relation, and fast, slow, and intermediate shocks by the magnitude or orientation of the $α$-normalised tangential branch difference. Perpendicular, parallel, switch-on, and switch-off shocks appear as geometrical or limiting cases. The resulting classification expresses the classical discontinuity conditions in a wave-aligned form and, through the characteristic interpretation of $\boldsymbol{Q}_0^{\pm}$, shows how ideal-MHD discontinuities constrain changes in characteristic propagation direction and speed across the interface. It therefore establishes the background interface structure required for subsequent studies of reflection, transmission, coupling, and mode conversion.
authors: Anna Krupka; Tom Van Doorsselaere

title: Polarized X-rays from table-top free-electron-driven van der Waals crystals
summary: Polarized X-rays are essential for polarization-sensitive techniques such as X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy, magnetic microscopy, and fluorescence imaging. These techniques are crucial in the study of molecular and material dynamics, which are in turn central to driving the global transition to clean energy and sustainability through research in photovoltaics, catalysis and optoelectronics. Currently, polarized X-rays with tunable polarization and photon energy are available only in large facilities like synchrotrons. Here, we theoretically predict and experimentally demonstrate the generation of linearly polarized X-rays from free electron-driven van der Waals crystals, without the need for additional optical stages like polarizers. We show that precise, real-time control over the polarization can be achieved by simply re-orienting the van der Waals crystal. Furthermore, we show that a high degree of polarization can be achieved across all polarization angles - from perpendicular to in-plane - with intensities exceeding 10^9 photons s^(-1) sr^(-1) mA^(-1). Using our findings, we present a scheme for table-top XANES, achieving performance comparable to that of synchrotron facilities. In the process, we develop a new methodology for performing XANES using high-quality polarized X-rays with larger spectral linewidths, named ORIXANES (Orientation-controlled XANES). Our findings pave the way to greater accessibility and smaller carbon footprint for advanced X-ray modalities.
authors: Nikhil Pramanik; Sunchao Huang; Ruihuan Duan; Lee Wei Wesley Wong; Qingwei Zhai; Wen Wei Lee; Zheng Liu; Liang Jie Wong

title: Development of an FPGA-Based Readout System and Functional Characterization of a Custom NSX1 ASIC for X-ray instrumentation
summary: We developed an FPGA-based readout system for a front-end ASIC (NSX1) with 64 channels to read out a large- area silicon drift detector used in X-ray detection instruments such as the Wide Field Monitor module for the STROBE-X mission concept. The FPGA acts as a central controller for the NSX1 configuration, implementing trigger handling and event sequencing, precise event timestamping, control of an external ADC for digitization, and data transfer to the host PC. The system enables comprehensive ASIC characterization; here, we demonstrate preliminary ASIC functionality and characterization tests using a calibrated pulser for two programmable linear gain responses of 375 mV/fC and 750 mV/fC. These preliminary results validate the low-noise performance of the NSX1 ASIC and demonstrate successful integration of the DAQ system.
authors: Nabin Poudyal; Wayne Baumgartner; Sukanya Chakrabarti; Gianluigi De Geronimo; Wesley Hodge; Peter Jenke; Paul Ray; Jarred Roberts; Eric Wulf

title: Optical imaging with only the evanescent fields and without diffraction
summary: We report on a conceptual framework for optical imaging utilizing exclusively evanescent fields, effectively eliminating or attenuating standard optical diffraction. We present the theoretical foundation of this concept based on the decomposition of dipole radiation into evanescent fields and homogeneous propagating waves, exploring the explicit conditions required to suppress the latter. By successfully decoupling and removing the homogeneous component, optical tasks, such as sub-diffraction imaging, can be executed solely via evanescent channels, bypassing traditional diffractive limits. We discuss the physical feasibility of this approach and provide concrete examples of how this conjecture can be realized using currently available laboratory and industrial techniques. The realization of this concept promises to redefine core paradigms in optics and fundamental physics. Because the minimum achievable feature size is no longer governed by the operating wavelength, this approach enables an unprecedented increase in spatial resolution, offering a direct pathway to advance state-of-the-art semiconductor lithography and chip manufacturing.
authors: Mufei Xiao

title: A Differentiable Framework for Inverse Identification of Heterogeneous Cohesive Laws
summary: This work develops a differentiable finite element framework based on an intrinsic cohesive-zone formulation for identifying traction-separation laws from global force-displacement histories and spatially sparse strain measurements. The framework employs physics-constrained neural networks to represent flexible, thermodynamically structured cohesive laws, with sensitivities computed through automatic differentiation and a discrete adjoint that accounts for the history-dependent evolution of interfacial damage. To enable identification of spatially heterogeneous cohesive behavior, we extend learned constitutive priors to irreversible interfacial damage by constructing a shared, low-dimensional family of cohesive laws from representative traction-separation histories. This representation exploits common constitutive structure and parameter sharing to reduce the number of unknowns and regularize the inverse problem, while allowing local cohesive behavior to vary spatially through latent coordinates. Numerical investigations involving double-cantilever beams and fiber-matrix composites demonstrate that accurate reproduction of global force-displacement responses does not necessarily imply accurate recovery of the underlying cohesive laws. Incorporating spatially resolved strain measurements substantially improves constitutive identification, even when the admissible responses are constrained by a learned prior. Comparisons with conventional bilinear cohesive models and Bayesian optimization further illustrate the benefits of the learned constitutive representation and adjoint-based identification for high-dimensional inverse problems.
authors: Sida Hao; Jinkyo Han; Bahador Bahmani

title: Deep-Microscopic Photonic Bandstructure of a Two-Dimensional Honeycomb Lattice
summary: Conventional descriptions of light in materials rely on macroscopic models that average the optical response over the microscopic lattice structures. These models are deployed in the semi-classical limit, where the collective local response over many lattice sites is adequate. However, they fail to capture the full spatial dispersion, which requires a lattice-resolved description of light. We address this limitation by formulating a deep-microscopic nonlocal theory of the photon based on the Maxwell Hamiltonian and its characteristic equation. The solution reveals the full spatial dispersion in the form of deep-microscopic photonic bandstructure, and corresponding real-space Bloch field textures. We demonstrate our theory for a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a gapped honeycomb lattice. Our framework thus extends photons to the same microscopic footing as electrons or phonons, providing a unified route to studying topology, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations of light in dispersive materials.
authors: Pronoy Das; Sathwik Bharadwaj; Wenbo Sun; Zubin Jacob

title: Walk on Multiscale Media: Compiling Editable and Composable Transport Medium Prefabs for Monte Carlo PDE Solvers
summary: Monte Carlo PDE solvers enable mesh-free pointwise queries, but repeatedly traversing heterogeneous media is costly, particularly in scenes with reusable or dynamically changing materials. We introduce Walk on Multiscale Media (WoMM), which compiles fine-scale transport into reusable, editable and composable transport prefabs. A probabilistic interpretation of multiscale finite-element bases and condensed operators yields coarse transitions retaining fine-scale material effects. Each prefab combines port-level operators, entrance-dependent exit distributions, and Poisson-marked trajectory records, enabling incremental updates for overlapping absorption fields, gradient-field steering through path reweighting and transient diffusion. Integrated with conventional Walk-on-Spheres in a hybrid continuous--discrete solver, these prefabs accelerate repeated pointwise PDE queries and support interactive material edits without repeatedly solving the fine-scale problem.
authors: Yunfeng Liao; Xiucheng Li

title: New constraints on holographic dark energy with high-redshift galaxy observations from JWST
summary: Observations of high-redshift galaxies from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) provide a complementary probe of early structure formation. Meanwhile, DESI results have provided further indications of possible dynamical dark energy, prompting investigations of theoretically motivated dark energy models. In this work, we investigate holographic dark energy (HDE) and interacting holographic dark energy (IHDE) using JWST ultraviolet luminosity function measurements, cosmic microwave background (CMB) observations from Planck and ACT, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation measurements, and DES-Dovekie type~Ia supernova data. We find that JWST has little impact on the parameter constraints of $Λ$CDM and HDE but produces more pronounced changes in those of IHDE. For CMB+DESI+DES-Dovekie, adding JWST shifts the holographic parameter $c$ from $1.270^{+0.146}_{-0.096}$ to $1.091\pm0.095$ and the interaction parameter $β$ from $0.650^{+0.104}_{-0.034}$ to $0.498^{+0.090}_{-0.061}$, accompanied by an increase in $Ω_{\rm m}$ and a decrease in $S_8$. For the full data combination, $χ^2_{\rm JWST}$ decreases by approximately $7$ for both HDE and IHDE compared with $Λ$CDM, indicating improved fits to the high-redshift galaxy abundances. Our results highlight the complementary role of high-redshift galaxy observations in probing the HDE and IHDE models.
authors: Sheng-Han Zhou; Tian-Nuo Li; Guo-Hong Du; Yi-Min Zhang; Yun-He Li; Jing-Fei Zhang; Xin Zhang

title: Triple Decomposition of Field Gradient Tensors in Space Plasmas
summary: Characterizing local topology in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is fundamental to understanding energy dissipation, intermittency, and coherent structures in space plasmas. Classical double decomposition of velocity ($A_{ij}$) and magnetic ($Z_{ij}$) field gradient tensors into symmetric strain and anti-symmetric rotation components conflates rigid-body rotation with planar sliding shear. Here, we extend the real-Schur-based Triple Decomposition framework to MHD flows, rigorously isolating irrotational normal strain ($N, M$), residual pure shear ($H, K$), and true rigid-body rotation ($R, B$). Applying this method to high-resolution NASA-MMS multi-spacecraft observations in the solar wind and Earth's magnetosheath reveals distinct topological signatures. Solar wind dynamics are predominantly strain-dominated due to spherical radial expansion, whereas magnetosheath turbulence is overwhelmingly shear-dominated, driven by boundary interactions. Crucially, cross-term contributions ($2RH$ and $2KB$) are suppressed to $\le 7\%$ across both plasma regimes, contrasting sharply with neutral fluid turbulence ($\sim 13\%$). This suppression is driven by background magnetic-field-induced anisotropy ($k_\perp \gg k_\parallel$), which confines shearing motions perpendicular to the primary rotation axes. By cleanly separating genuine vortex cores from current sheets and shear layers, the Triple Decomposition provides an objective framework for characterizing plasma turbulence and analyzing data from future multi-spacecraft missions.
authors: Virgilio Quattrociocchi; Giuseppe Consolini; Maria Federica Marcucci

title: Accelerating high-fidelity gyrokinetic fusion simulations with iGENE
summary: We present the latest version of iGENE, a differentiable implementation of the local (flux-tube) gyrokinetic code GENE, now fully rewritten in JAX. iGENE features a multispecies, collisional, fully electromagnetic nonlinear gyrokinetic model while preserving end-to-end differentiability. The code is verified against GENE for linear ITG, TEM and KBM physics and for nonlinear turbulent fluxes with adiabatic and kinetic electrons. Forward-mode derivatives of the linear growth rate agree with finite differences for all five parameters tested, resolving the 30--50\% discrepancy in $\hat{s}$ and $ε$ reported for the earlier TensorFlow version. All collectives are native JAX operations, and the code strong-scales from 2 to 32 H100 GPUs with 86\% parallel efficiency. We then assess three routes to a shorter time to solution. Custom CUDA FFT kernels operating in bfloat16 are up to $3.97\times$ faster than fp32 cuFFT on the transforms, and on a single H100 iGENE is $2.63\times$ faster per time step than single-precision GENE. Multi-rate sub-cycling of the parallel dynamics yields a further $1.89\times$ speedup with kinetic electrons. Finally, a Hermite-Laguerre velocity-space representation is implemented, offering tunable fidelity.
authors: Gabriele Merlo; Victor Artigues; Carl-Martin Pfeiler; Frank Jenko

title: Long-Baseline Phase-Coherent Microwave Reception Using Rydberg Atoms
summary: A long baseline phase-coherent microwave receiver is demonstrated using a remotely interrogated cesium Rydberg atom sensor over an 8 m free-space optical link. A 3.989 GHz local oscillator (LO) is intensity-modulated onto an 852 nm optical probe and recovered remotely for atomic superheterodyne detection. A 509 nm coupling laser establishes a Rydberg electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) system addressing the 6S1/2 to 6P3/2 to 56D5/2 ladder, with microwave coupling to 57P3/2. A test signal offset by 5 kHz generates an optically detected intermediate-frequency (IF) response returned to the reference station for centralized coherent acquisition. This eliminates independent remote oscillators, electronic IF acquisition, and distributed clock synchronization. Over 10 min, the differential phase between remote and local reference exhibits a standard deviation of 0.476 deg and a minimum overlapping phase Allan deviation of 0.048 deg at approximately 200 s averaging. Following optical-link interruption, the differential phase recovers without recalibration, with a measured pre- and post-interruption difference of 0.01 deg. These results demonstrate phase coherent remotely interrogated atomic microwave reception with reduced instrumentation, supporting future distributed interferometry, multistatic radar, and coherent sensor arrays.
authors: Darmindra Arumugam; Brook Feyissa

title: A Novel Linked-Mirror Device for Fusion
summary: We design a novel linked-mirror device (LMD) with a magnetic well using the near-axis expansion (NAE) method. The design consists of two parallel straight mirror sections connected at both ends by three-dimensional stellarator-like magnetic fields , thereby eliminating the end-loss problem of a single magnetic mirror. By designing appropriate three-dimensional magnetic fields, we obtain an LMD configuration with a magnetic well, ensuring stability against interchange modes. The existence of finite-\b{eta} equilibria of the LMD is demonstrated by numerical solutions of the 3D equilibrium code GVEC. This design is potentially a novel solution to magnetic confinement for fusion reactors.
authors: Haorong Qiu; Xiang Li; Guodong Yu; Zhexuan Zheng; Caoxiang Zhu; Guoyong Fu

title: Six-Degree-of-Freedom Rotor-Load Cross-Spectral Density from Rotor-Plane Turbulence Cross-Spectra
summary: A frequency-domain response analysis of a wind turbine rotor requires the complete hub-load spectrum, but the customary scalar thrust and torque spectra retain neither the four in-plane components nor the coupling between them. This paper derives the full six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) rotor-load cross-spectral-density (CSD) matrix from the IEC Kaimal turbulence model. By decoupling the spatial order of inflow coherence from the temporal Doppler shift, the formulation introduces a two-index rotational-sampling kernel. Rotor symmetry and azimuthal averaging constrain the observed Doppler carrier strictly to blade-passing harmonics $pBf_{\mathrm{rot}}$, while the azimuthal aerodynamic transfer shifts the spatial coherence order to $pB+s$. A convergence study of the retained azimuthal order $s$ shows that $\lvert s\rvert\le4$ suffices, the assembled CSD then deviating from the full-band result by less than $10^{-5}$ in relative norm. The formulation is compared with OpenFAST simulations of a rigid floating wind turbine over nine wind speeds: the six auto-spectral densities agree closely below 1~Hz, and the present theory over-predicts the spectra near the 6P and 9P rotational harmonics.
authors: Haoran Yang; Zhaolong Han

title: Polarization-resolved haze in transparent wood - towards wooden glass
summary: Transparent wood (TW) composites possess residual haze that limits image clarity despite their high light transmission, yet the physical origin of this scattering has not been established. Here, polarization-resolved measurements reveal a pronounced polarization dependence of scattering by a wood-polymer composite with improved refractive index matching. Polarization- and spectrally-resolved haze as low as 21% (40-45% at 550 nm for unpolarized light) with transmittance of approximately 92% for polarization perpendicular to the fibers was detected. It is found that the low-haze spectrum closely follows an inverse-square relation over the 400-800 nm range, well described by a weak-index-contrast Rayleigh-Gans-Debye (RGD) model invoking subwavelength birefringent heterogeneities within the cell wall. This physical mechanism was previously obscured by haze-limiting strong scattering from debonding gaps or refraction at the lumen-cell wall interface. Scanning electron diffraction independently reveals spatially distinct domains with markedly different cellulose diffraction responses within the infiltrated cell walls. The observed polarization-dependent refractive-index mismatch is attributed to inherent cellulose birefringence. Time-resolved measurements further support nearly scattering-free quasi-ballistic transport of the sampled transmitted light. It is demonstrated that selecting only a preferential polarization markedly improves image visibility through TW without further material modification. These findings connect polarization-dependent haze to the internal structure of transparent wood and identify ways to engineer a refractive-index match in hierarchical anisotropic composites towards glass-like clarity.
authors: Zheheng Song; Hui Chen; Mathias Nero; Jingjian Zhou; Ravi Shanker; Tom Willhammar; Lars Berglund; Ilya Sychugov

title: Relativistic Cavity Quantum Electrodynamical Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Method for Strong Light-Matter Coupling
summary: We present the relativistic four-component implementation of cavity quantum electrodynamical algebraic diagrammatic construction theory at second order (4c-QED-EE-ADC(2)) for the ab initio treatment of light-matter interactions. Starting from the unitary-transformed, origin-invariant Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian, a rigorous four-component Dirac-Hartree-Fock formulation including cavity effects is considered, forming the basis of the 4c-QED-EE-ADC(2) framework. Two variants are implemented, allowing cavity effects to be introduced either at the relativistic mean-field or exclusively at the electron-correlation level. Applications to Hg, AuH, and halogen hydrides demonstrate that cavity coupling significantly modifies relativistic excitation spectra, induces strong state mixing, and enables tunable polaritonic features. Potential energy surface calculations for HBr further reveal cavity-induced qualitative changes in excited-state surfaces. It is also observed that the inclusion of photonic degrees of freedom leads to a moderate computational overhead of approximately three to five times relative to standard 4c-EE-ADC(2).
authors: Sudipta Chakraborty; Amrita Manna; Lukas Konecny; Achintya Kumar Dutta

title: Ground-motion simulation of multi-segment ruptures on the Alpine-Marlborough fault system
summary: The Alpine Fault (AF) is the major plate boundary crustal structure in New Zealand (NZ), producing large-to-great (M7-8+) earthquakes approximately every 300-500 years, and has long been a focal point for earthquake resilience in NZ. This study advances prior AF ground-motion modelling by considering multi-segment ruptures that initiate on the AF and rupture northward onto structures in the Marlborough Fault Zone (MFZ), resulting in ground shaking of consequential amplitudes for the upper South Island and Lower North Island, including Wellington city. From the 2022 NZ National Seismic Hazard Model (NSHM), three multi-segment rupture geometries including the Wairau, Clarence, and Hope fault structures in the MFZ are obtained, together with their scenario rupture rates. Hybrid broadband simulations using a multi-segment kinematic source description and a 3D NZ crustal velocity model are performed. Three rupture realizations per geometry are considered to compare the effects of kinematic rupture randomness with those of the different geometries. To provide comparisons with the prior ground-motion simulations used for public outreach in the AF8 programme, we also simulated the segmented M7.9 Alpine Fiordland-to-Kelly rupture geometry of Bradley et al. (2017a), adopting the same southern hypocentre location in all rupture scenarios, enabling examination of differences due to eight years of advancements in kinematic rupture and crustal velocity modelling. Results illustrate strong northward directivity and basin response, with the largest Wellington amplitudes resulting from the Alpine-Wairau and Alpine-Clarence scenarios -- peak ground accelerations of approximately 0.1 g, comparable to those observed during the 2016 Kaikōura earthquake; in aggregate, these Alpine-MFZ ruptures have a likelihood similar to the conventionally-considered Wellington Fault and Hikurangi subduction sources.
authors: Brendon A. Bradley; Jake Faulkner; Felipe Kuncar; Cesar A. Pajaro

title: An In-depth Study of Stochastic Stellarator Coil Optimization
summary: We extend stochastic coil optimization for stellarators and analyze the effect of optimizing for coil manufacturing errors, assembly errors represented by centroid translations and angular offsets, and errors in the coil currents. We further analyze the impact of different perturbation methods and use them in conjunction with the Augmented Lagrangian algorithm. For three stellarators, we show that stochastic methods regularize the coil optimization landscape and improve robustness in every case, with the magnitude of the improvement varying substantially across different plasmas. Our metric for coil robustness, $Q$, is improved by $4.50\%$ to $729\%$ across different configurations. Lastly, we perform numerous hyperparameter scans, including e.g. scanning the training perturbation size and the out-of-sample (OOS) evaluation perturbation size and find coupled and de-coupled training tolerance gains ranging from $0.09$ mm to $1.35$ mm depending strongly on the particular stellarator.
authors: Vincenzo Gallegos; Evan Laljit; Julianne Stratton; Gabe Perez-Giz; Alan Kaptanoglu

title: Contact-Free Nuclear and Cytoplasmic Mechanophenotyping by Amplitude-Modulated Ultrasound and Phase-Locked Optical Diffraction Tomography: Computational Feasibility and Initial Experimental Readouts
summary: We investigate whether acoustic stimulation combined with phase-locked optical diffraction tomography (ODT) could measure the mechanical responses of the nucleus and cytoplasm separately in adherent cells. A megahertz ultrasound carrier is amplitude-modulated at low frequencies, while angle-scanned holography provides a route to reconstruct the first-harmonic refractive-index response in three dimensions. We built a computational model connecting viscoelastic finite-element simulations of MDA-MB-231 cells with a refractive-index phantom, hologram formation, camera noise and ODT reconstruction. Under an assumed 0.1 Pa harmonic shear traction at 10 Hz, the model predicts 3.6 to 9.2 nm of nuclear shear and 6.6 to 15.1 nm of apical motion. The nuclear-to-cytoplasmic amplitude ratio (R_A) is primarily sensitive to stiffness contrast in the tested scenarios, while the relative phase (Delta phi) responds to differences in dissipation. A simulated protocol using 100 illumination angles and 16 phase visits per angle recovered an imposed stiffening and recovery trajectory after averaging four acquisitions. We also obtained initial 3D tomograms of adherent MDA-MB-231 cells and report preliminary regional measurements from five cells. Their mean amplitude ratio was 0.616 plus or minus 0.098, and their mean relative phase was -1.91 plus or minus 0.58 degrees (mean and between-cell sample standard deviation). All five amplitude ratios were below unity, and all phase differences were negative, consistent with the qualitative directions of selected model scenarios. The small cohort and the absence of independently quantified experimental phase noise prevent a claim of quantitative mechanical validation. Together, these results support further evaluation of phase-locked acoustic ODT and identify experimental requirements for a controlled validation study.
authors: Yagmur Isik; Merve Sevgi; Esmahan Caglar; Aysenur Akgun; Hasan Berkay Abdioglu; Gokhan Bora Esmer; Huseyin Uvet

title: A neural accelerated roughness-resolved Discrete Element Method (Rough-DEM) for modeling granular systems
summary: The Discrete Element Method (DEM) is an indispensable tool for modeling and understanding the basic mechanical behaviors of (dry) granular media, a class of disordered material systems of significant interest to multiple scientific domains from (geo-)physics to (chemical) engineering. At the core of all present DEM frameworks is a phenomenological friction law--commonly chosen to be of the Amontons-Coulomb type--that models the frictional interaction among constituent grains. Here, inspired by research in the tribology community, we present an alternative, fundamentally different framework, termed roughness-resolved DEM (Rough-DEM), in which contact friction is handled in a more physics-based manner. In this framework, instead of using a friction law, we explicitly resolve the surface topography of each grain and let friction emerge from collective frictionless interactions of surface asperities. In essence, we trade phenomenology for physics at the cost of an increased computational demand. To mitigate the cost, we introduce an FE$^2$-like algorithm and a feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM)-based neural network surrogate, both of which are parallelized on GPU to accelerate contact computation. Crucially, using this framework in 2D, we (1) demonstrate the possibility of recovering a two-body-based Amontons-Coulomb-type friction behavior using a \textit{simple} representation of surface topography, and (2) identify many-body-based frictional behaviors--more specifically, the angle of repose values--that \textit{cannot always} be captured by current DEM frameworks under the same level of model complexity. We conclude by discussing future directions for Rough-DEM, as well as exciting new opportunities it could unlock for a wide range of emerging applications, including (designing) suspension rheology and metamaterial mechanics.
authors: Xiwei Pan; Liuchi Li

title: Loss Factor of Axisymmetric and Rectangular Tapered Collimators from Optical to Inductive Regimes
summary: In this work, we investigate the loss factor of axisymmetric and rectangular tapered collimators over a broad range of bunch lengths and geometrical parameters using the electromagnetic simulation codes ECHO and GdfidL. The calculations are performed for Gaussian bunches of rms length $σ_s$, with the collimator geometry characterized by the minimum and maximum apertures $b$ and $d$, taper length $L$, and chamber width $W$ for rectangular structures. For short bunches and tapered collimators with $d-b>b$, we extend the phenomenological formula previously obtained for axisymmetric to rectangular tapered collimators, describing the dependence of the loss factor on bunch length and taper geometry through an arctangent function of the scaling parameter $μd^2/(σ_s L)$. We demonstrate that this parameter is related to a Fresnel number and, by combining diffraction theory with the electrodynamics of the beam-induced image charge, analytically explain the factor of two between the coefficients $μ=0.2$ and $μ=0.4$ for axisymmetric and rectangular collimators, respectively. The resulting expression is applicable to rectangular collimators with $W/(2d) \geq 1.8$, extending its validity beyond the idealized flat geometry. For longer bunches, we identify the transition from the optical to the inductive regime and derive an analytical expression for the loss factor based on the cutoff wavenumber of the lowest relevant electromagnetic mode.
authors: Md Wahidur Rahman; Alexei Blednykh; Gang Wang; Xiaofeng Gu

title: Autonomous atomistic-continuum coupling through uncertainty-aware active learning
summary: We develop an uncertainty-aware surrogate modeling approach for coupling an atomistic kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) surface-chemistry solver with a continuum multi-species fluid dynamics solver across disparate physical length and time scales. The surrogate model predicts boundary mass fluxes for six species and their uncertainties, which the continuum solver monitors to automatically trigger additional KMC simulations when new training data are needed. This enables efficient multiscale coupling and maintains a user-specified level of accuracy. We demonstrate the approach for reactive halide-perovskite vapor deposition, which involves a multi-species vapor jet impinging on a reactive substrate. The KMC solver uses a DFT-calibrated energetics model that we construct as part of this work and provides net deposition and desorption rates for six species. With a conservative uncertainty threshold, the surrogate-coupled approach reproduces cumulative mass fluxes of the directly coupled approach with errors typically within 10-20%, while capturing the non-monotonic dependence of net deposition on species partial pressure. Importantly, the results show that detailed crystal structure need not be explicitly represented to predict quantities exchanged between atomistic and continuum solvers; species-resolved mass fluxes provide a sufficiently low-dimensional representation of the atomistic response. For this accuracy target, the autonomous online-learning approach reduces the number of required atomistic simulations by two to three orders of magnitude relative to direct multiscale coupling.
authors: Daniel Abdulah; Hariswaran Sitaraman; Ross E. Larsen; Kevin Patrick Griffin; Grace Wei; Janelle Domantay; Ethan Young; Marc T. Henry de Frahan

title: Predicting the onset of airfoil stall in transitional and turbulent flows with a pressure-gradient-based separation model for RANS simulations
summary: We propose an improved version of the $k$-$ω$ shear-stress transport Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes model that supersedes our prior work (Griffin et al. 2024 J. Turb.) with an updated pressure-gradient sensor that generalizes well across geometries and to laminar, transitional, and turbulent flows alike. The model is based on a composite pressure gradient criterion that uses the solution of an intermittency transport equation to synthesize the separation criteria of the Falkner-Skan theory for laminar flows and the continuously critical theory for turbulent flows. The proposed model is applied to various airfoils including the thick airfoils representative of wind turbine applications (DU00-w-212, S809 and S814) and thinner airfoils used in aerospace applications [NACA23012 and NLF(1)-0416]. For all airfoils, the proposed model is found to preserve or improve the predictions of the baseline model for both fully turbulent and transitional airfoils as demonstrated with results for the lift and drag coefficients. The model is also found to improve the prediction of separation on the NREL Phase VI rotor in a preliminary study, suggesting that the model will generalize to other complex three-dimensional flows.
authors: Kevin Patrick Griffin; Bumseok Lee; Ganesh Vijayakumar; Benjamin Savino; Brett J. Bornhoft; Omkar B. Shende; Michael P. Whitmore

title: Cavity Loss in QED Coupled-Cluster Theory: Polariton Linewidths, Driven Steady States, and the Rabi Splitting
summary: Molecular polariton experiments are performed in lossy cavities, whereas correlated ab initio polariton theory has been developed almost entirely for lossless cavities. In this work, cavity loss is added to real-time QED coupled-cluster theory (QED-CCSD-22) through a complex cavity frequency, which gives the non-Hermitian no-jump part of the Lindblad master equation. The resulting polariton linewidths and driven-dissipative steady states are, to our knowledge, the first from QED coupled-cluster theory. The linewidths obtained from the complex Jacobian and from real-time propagation agree and are partitioned by the biorthogonal photon numbers of the two polaritons. A closed-form continuous-wave drive of the cavity gives driven steady states and their lineshapes.
authors: Kurt R. Brorsen

title: Inverse Reconstruction of Double Imaging Schlieren
summary: Double imaging is a common artefact in off-axis single-mirror Schlieren systems. Depending on the distance between the object of interest and the mirror, together with the off-axis imaging geometry, such systems often capture images containing a superposition of the target image and a displaced ghost image, resulting in the so-called double imaging phenomenon. This not only degrades image quality, but also complicates its interpretation. To address this problem, we present a new model for ghost image displacement that takes into consideration finite-aperture support, defocus, and magnification. We then use this model to reconstruct the target image via total variation regularisation with a matrix-free alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Extensive experiments using both synthetic and real Schlieren images validate the proposed model, show the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm, and evaluate its performance under parameter mismatch. The proposed framework provides a computational alternative to hardware-based suppression of double imaging, enabling physics-consistent reconstruction while preserving the simplicity and compactness of off-axis single-mirror Schlieren systems.
authors: Shubham Saxena; João F. C. Mota

title: Flow Mesh: A Velocity-Regularized Flow Matching Framework for Stable Distributional Modeling of Physical Fields on Unstructured Meshes
summary: Thermal-fluid field distributions underpin the analysis and operation of energy infrastructure, from nuclear-reactor cooling channels to industrial heat exchangers, but resolving these distributions through computational fluid dynamics requires prohibitively large simulation ensembles. Their complex geometries also demand unstructured meshes that are poorly accommodated by generative models developed for regular grids. Here we introduce FlowMesh, a generative framework that combines permutation-invariant mesh encoding with deterministic latent flow matching and an l1 penalty on the learned transport velocity. FlowMesh generates full-field realizations directly on fixed unstructured meshes without auxiliary grid interpolation or a stochastic denoising chain. Across lid-driven-cavity, pressurized-water-reactor subchannel and heat-exchanger datasets, evaluated over six matched training seeds, FlowMesh achieves macro-averaged probability-density-function coverage of 91.7%-97.0%, exceeding an architecture-controlled latent diffusion model by $11.6$--$45.4$ percentage points. Latent-velocity regularization increases coverage by $3.8$ percentage points for reactor flows and 1.1 points for heat-exchanger flows, while reducing temperature-field Kullback--Leibler divergence by 1.7-2.4-fold. Each full-field realization requires 1.23 \pm 0.15 s, providing a 585--1902-fold wall-clock acceleration over computational fluid dynamics. FlowMesh therefore makes large-scale generative characterization of thermal-fluid states computationally feasible, providing a foundation for data-driven analysis and digital-twin development in fixed-geometry energy systems.
authors: Siddharth Verma; Jaewan Park; Jay Phil Yoo; Kazuma Kobayashi; Souvik Chakraborty; Syed Bahauddin Alam

title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
summary: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.
authors: Maxime Chambonneau; Mario Garcia-Lechuga; David Grojo; Stefan Nolte

title: Single-molecule cold chemistry: Isotopic branching ratios of the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction at cryogenic temperatures
summary: Isotopic branching in ion-molecule reactions influences interstellar deuterium fractionation, yet its dynamics remain poorly understood for many important systems at astrophysically relevant temperatures. Here, we investigate H- and D-atom transfer in the $\mathrm{H_2O^+ + HD}$ reaction using single sympathetically cooled water ions in a cryogenic radiofrequency trap. Nondestructive identification of the products from 441 individual reaction events at a mean collision energy of 7 K reveals an $\mathrm{H_3O^+/H_2DO^+}$ product branching ratio of $1.50 \pm 0.15$ demonstrating a preferential H-atom transfer. The experiments are rationalized using quasi-classical-trajectory calculations which indicate a transition from direct dynamics at higher energies to a complex-mediated reaction under the present experimental conditions and point to an important role of intramolecular vibrational redistribution affecting the isotopic branching in this regime. The present results extend measurements into an astrochemically relevant energy regime and establish cryogenic single-ion chemistry as a new platform for resolving competing reaction pathways.
authors: Nanditha Sunil Kumar; Prerna Paliwal; Mikhail Popov; Xueyi Li; Anyang Li; Hua Guo; Stefan Willitsch

title: A classical trajectory method for diatom-atom-atom ternary association reactions
summary: We introduce a classical trajectory method for calculating direct diatom-atom-atom ternary association re- action rates that incorporates the rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic reactant. By treating the diatomic molecule as a rigid rotor, we include the effects of the anisotropy of the molecule-atom interaction and the dynamical effects of the rotational motion. We apply this approach to a system of experimental interest, CD+ + He + He, along with the isotopic variant CH+ + He + He -> CHHe+ + He, and examine the role of the internal, rotational degrees of freedom of the diatomic molecule. In particular, we find that in the regime where the collision energy is much smaller than the rotational energy of the entrance channel, the rotational motion leads to deviation from the classical threshold law by violating the assumptions of long-range capture theory models.
authors: Daniel Julian; Jesus Perez-Rios

title: Polarization-encoded photon statistics for counting dipole emitters
summary: Counting the emitters within a diffraction-limited region is a prerequisite for localizing overlapping molecules. Under pulsed excitation, each molecule emits at most one photon per pulse, so photon-number-resolved detection can count emitters without resolving them. But the required number of pulses grows steeply with the emitter number. Here we show that polarization, conventionally used to measure the orientations of dipole emitters, also carries information on their number. Because mean polarization-resolved signals are unchanged when every emitter is replaced by multiple dimmer copies, this information resides in the photon statistics within each pulse, which polarization reshapes in two ways. Linearly polarized excitation at three angles increases the sub-Poissonian deficit of the photon count by a factor of 1.5 for any emitter orientation, and detection in four polarization channels reveals the emitter number through how the photons of multiphoton pulses are distributed among the channels. Maximum-likelihood simulations for two to five emitters of unknown orientations and brightnesses show that three-angle excitation reduces the required number of pulses by about 2.3-fold, close to the predicted $1.5^2=2.25$, and that adding four-channel detection raises the reduction to as much as 4.8-fold. These gains require only polarization optics added to photon-number-resolved detection.
authors: Oumeng Zhang

title: The scintillating fibre beam monitor for the CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS: characterisation of the light collection and detection system
summary: The CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS aims at a non-destructive isotopic characterisation of lead samples, based on muonic atom formation. A custom scintillation-based detector is used for the reconstruction of the time and space distributions of the low-energy muon beam employed in the experiment. The beam monitor consists of two orthogonal planes of 10 cm-long, 3 mm $\times$ 3 mm square scintillating fibres, totalling 64 fibres, read out by four arrays of 16 Hamamatsu S14160-3015PS SiPMs each. The optical performance of the detector has been characterised, focusing on the SiPM behaviour, and also checking and correcting the uniformity of the light response across channels with a $^{60}$ Co source. A first detector test with protons at the CNAO-XPR has been carried out. The results of the Geant4 simulation of the detector, fundamental for the detector operation and data analysis, are also presented. All these activities are preliminary to the final detector operation in the CHNet-MAXI experiment at the RIKEN-RAL Port4 decay muon beamline at ISIS.
authors: Lisa Malliolio; Riccardo Rossini; Andrea Abba; Roberto Bertoni; Sayani Biswas; Matteo Cataldo; Giancarlo Ceruti; Carlo De Vecchi; Daniela Di Martino; Adrian D. Hillier; James S. Lord; Giulia Marcucci; Alessandro Menegolli; Alessio Mereghetti; Paola Monza; Maya Musa; Piernicola Oliva; Federico Palenzona; Maurizio Perego; Daniel E. Pooley; Marco C. Prata; Marco Pullia; Lina Quintieri; Maria Pia Riccardi; Alice Roggio; Massimo Rossella; Simone Savazzi; Valeria Sipala; Erik S. Vallazza; Claudio Viviani; Massimiliano Clemenza

title: Radiation damage and recovery of SiPMs exposed to low-momentum muon beams for innovative scintillation-based muon beam monitors
summary: Silicon PhotoMultipliers (SiPMs) are among the standard devices for light detection in scintillator detectors. Some detector designs require these devices to be placed in radioactive areas or directly exposed to particle beams. Specifically, the damage from exposure to low-momentum muons is particularly important, as they have a high energy deposit and they have several applications in material science and particle physics. Eight SiPM models from different manufacturers were exposed to 29 MeV/c positive muons, with an intensity of O(10^6) muons/s for 13 hours, maximising the charge deposited in the depletion region. I-V curves were measured before/after irradiation and annealing; DCR and crosstalk analyses are ongoing, to extract dark count rate and optical crosstalk. Despite showing a measurable increase in dark current, the devices preserved operational stability. Thermal annealing has also been tested by heating the devices at 125°C, showing a recovery of the optimal SiPM features. This work is part of a collaboration between the University of Pavia and ISIS, to develop detectors for low-momentum muons (< 40 MeV/c), based on thin scintillators.
authors: Riccardo Rossini; Sayani Biswas; Adrian D. Hillier; James S. Lord; Lisa Malliolio; Alessandro Menegolli; William Mourad; Daniel E. Pooley; Marco C. Prata; Lina Quintieri; Massimo Rossella; Francesco Zamperoni

title: Quantum Index Report 2026
summary: The MIT Quantum Index Report 2026 provides a comprehensive, data-driven assessment of the evolving quantum-technology landscape. As quantum technologies progress from scientific promise toward practical deployment, decision-makers need clear, accessible measures of technical capability, investment, workforce development, policy and public engagement. This second edition expands and updates the Quantum Index Report's analysis of quantum computing and networking. It tracks developments across research, industry, education, government and society. Drawing on academic, commercial, and policy sources, the report synthesizes trends and visualizes change over time to support informed comparison and discussion. The Quantum Index Report is intended as a nonpartisan public resource for business leaders, educators, policymakers, researchers and the broader public. Its aim is to reduce the complexity of a rapidly changing field while clarifying both its opportunities and remaining challenges.
authors: Jonathan Ruane; Elif Kiesow; Carl Dukatz; Laura Converso

title: A Compact Single-Beam Optically Pumped Magnetometer Based on Absorption Detection
summary: We demonstrate a compact single-beam optically pumped magnetometer (OPM) employing a pure 87Rb microfabricated vapor cell with 500 Torr buffer gas. The residual magnetic field is actively minimized to below 400 pT through a combination of mu-metal magnetic shielding and internal compensation coils. We systematically characterize the OPM response as a function of laser detuning and optical intensity, and derive the magnetic-field sensitivity from the signal slope and noise amplitude spectral density. A best sensitivity of 11 fT/Hz^1/2 is achieved near the resonance transition at an optimal optical intensity, using a small cell volume of only 0.027 cm^3. Furthermore, a miniaturized OPM prototype was developed using a folded flexible printed circuit board (FPCB) to integrate the vapor cell, a compact heater, and magnetic-field coils into a cubic sensing head. Two coil configurations patterned directly on the FPCB were investigated. Under optimized operating conditions, the OPM prototype achieved a sensitivity of 66 fT/Hz^1/2. These results demonstrate that high-buffer-pressure single-beam OPMs can achieve excellent sensitivity, establishing a pathway toward compact and scalable arrays.
authors: Jia-You Liou; Yi-Hsuan Chen; Hsiang-An Chuang; Chih-Hsuan Huang; Zong-Hsin Liu; I-Chiao Tsai; Kai-Hsin Peng; Yi-Hsin Chen

title: Video-rate quantitative phase and polarimetric imaging (QP2I) for label-free imaging of contracting muscle cells
summary: Quantitative phase imaging (QPI) has become a standard approach for label-free microscopy of transparent specimens, mapping the optical path length. However, the isotropic phase is blind to the molecular order underlying optical anisotropy. Implementations that also add quantitative contrast to birefringence rely on multi-frame illumination or polarization-state scanning, or on dedicated interferometric hardware and thus trade away acquisition speed or the simplicity of a standard microscope. We present Quantitative Phase and Polarimetric Imaging (QPPI), a computational imaging framework that converts a standard differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope with a polarization camera into a single-shot, video-rate, dual-contrast imaging system. We developed a new globally regularized phase reconstruction that eliminates artifacts of prior DIC-to-QPI approaches, providing quantitative phase information, and used per-pixel Stokes-based reconstruction to obtain quantitative anisotropic retardance. We validate the approach across simulations, static reference targets, fixed muscle tissue and living dynamically moving cells. QPPI enables all-optical and label-free studies of contractile dynamics in live cardiomyocytes. It provides both structural and functional readouts at sufficient frame rates to resolve fast cardiomyocyte contractions. Conventional fluorescent labels bleach over time, perturb physiology, and preclude long-term monitoring. Instead, QPPI enables long-term, label-free interrogation of dynamic cellular processes at quantitative contrast and provides structural readouts similar to those provided by established fluorescent labels, such as frame-by-frame sarcomere length. It also offers previously inaccessible measurements, like quantitative analysis of retardance changes during muscle contraction, which provides a direct optical signature of muscle photoelasticity.
authors: Lucas Kreiss Roohian; Nachiket Pathak; David Ripp; Mitchell Harling; Nils M. Kronenberg; Marcel Schubert; Malte C. Gather

title: Integrated elliptical III-V nanopillar arrays on silicon for dual photodetection and light emission
summary: Next-generation on-chip photonic devices require compact, energy-efficient components integrating photodetection and light emission on silicon platforms. Achieving broadband photodetection combined with efficient emission in a single nanoscale device remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate elliptical nanopillar arrays monolithically integrated as III-V-on-Si templates, exhibiting broadband photoresponse across visible to near-infrared wavelengths, dynamic neuron-like graded responses under modulated light, and pronounced electroluminescence at around 865 nm under forward bias. The nanostructured elliptical geometry approach enhances optical absorption and carrier dynamics within an active area significantly smaller than commercial detectors, enabling responsivities up to 0.55 A/W at 830 nm in compact nanoarrays. This work advances the development of miniaturized active nanophotonic devices suitable for integrated sensing, emitting and communication circuits, and neuromorphic processing on silicon substrates.
authors: João D. G. Azevedo; Rafael Ramos Uña; Ángela Barreda; Stuart Edwards; J. Iwan Davies; Jérôme Borme; Braulio Garcia-Cámara; Jana B. Nieder; Bruno Romeira

title: The Butterfly Defects: Tracing Cooperation in LLM Agent Networks
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate as interconnected agents, a fundamental question emerges: does individual cooperation translate into collective cooperation? We investigate this question through the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD), moving from dyadic interactions to homogeneous and heterogeneous networks of open-weight LLMs. Our findings reveal that cooperation is highly sensitive to model composition and seemingly minor linguistic changes. Models that cooperate with identical peers can shift toward defection in mixed populations. A simple uncertainty cue can increase or decrease cooperation, redistribute costs, and affect unexposed agents several hops away. Even reversing action-label order can dramatically alter behavior, with uncertainty framing sometimes amplifying this sensitivity. Together, these findings challenge the notion of cooperation as a stable model-level property, revealing how strategic behavior depends on interaction partners, network positions, and the language used to frame decisions.
authors: Maria Sampani; Maria Lymperaiou; Angeliki Dimitriou; Giorgos Filandrianos; Chrysoula Zerva; Giorgos Stamou

title: Supercontinuum-driven broadband Fourier-transform photothermal microspectroscopy
summary: Chemical characterization of microscopic samples often requires resolving multiple, widely separated vibrational absorption bands, including their positions and spectral shapes. Photothermal microspectroscopy provides a route to localized vibrational measurements by detecting absorption-induced thermal responses with a separate optical probe. However, rapid acquisition of broadband photothermal spectra remains challenging when spectral information is collected through sequential wavelength tuning. Here, we develop a supercontinuum (SC)-driven Fourier-transform photothermal (FT-PT) microspectroscopy platform that combines broadband near-infrared excitation with rapid-scan interferometric acquisition for localized vibrational measurements. In this approach, an interferometrically modulated SC pump induces wavelength-dependent photothermal responses in the sample, which are detected through a co-propagating visible probe beam and reconstructed by Fourier transformation. Using a 1.65-2.35 um spectral window, we demonstrate broadband photothermal spectra of aqueous samples with acquisition rates of approximately one spectrum per second. The system simultaneously resolves multiple molecular absorption features in a water-dimethyl sulfoxide mixture and reproduces the near-infrared absorption characteristics of liquid water with high spectral fidelity. Extending beyond homogeneous liquids, a dark-field detection configuration enables broadband photothermal spectroscopy of an individual 6 um polystyrene particle in an aqueous environment. This SC-based FT-PT microspectroscopy approach provides a rapid and broadband platform for localized vibrational characterization of liquid and microscopic samples, enabling chemical analysis with microscale spatial selectivity.
authors: Senyu Wang; Zicong Xu; Kazuki Hashimoto; Jianfeng Li; Takuro Ideguchi

title: The Dst index - empirical fits and temporal correlations
summary: Here I show how it is possible to make an empirical fit of yearly sets of Dst index values to the log-normal distribution, using the Kullback-Liebler divergence to test each fit performance. Further, since any real sequence of Dst values contains correlation with the near-past, I also compute autocorrelations in order to understand the timescales over which it retains memory.
authors: Paul Kinsler

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
